code.title: Role assignments flow down the Azure scope tree

followUps:
Use separate subscriptions for production and non-production. A subscription is a hard boundary for billing, quotas, policy and access, so a mistake in test cannot touch production.

Resource groups only group by life cycle; an Owner on a shared subscription can still reach everything inside it. Example: one subscription per environment (sub-prod, sub-test), each with one resource group per app. Use resource groups to separate environments only for tiny teams and prototypes.

A role assignment says who may do what; Azure Policy says what is allowed to exist, no matter who asks.

Example: a developer with Contributor can create a VM, but a policy that only allows the region westeurope will deny it in eastus. Policy can deny, audit, or auto-add things such as tags. Roles are about identities; policy is about resource properties. You normally need both.

Almost everything that is scoped to one tenant stops at its edge: you cannot assign a role to a user from tenant A on a resource in tenant B without making them a guest (B2B) or using Azure Lighthouse, a managed identity cannot be used in another tenant, and a policy or management group does not span tenants.

Each tenant has its own users, groups, app registrations and conditional access rules. Multi-tenant apps register once and get a service principal in each customer tenant.

Because a second region costs about double and adds real complexity: data replication, failover logic, testing and often higher latency between writes.

Example: a service that is allowed 4 hours of downtime a year may be fine with zone redundancy in one region (which survives a data centre failure). Go multi-region only when the business impact of a whole-region outage is higher than the extra cost and the extra moving parts.

Five things mainly: where the users and data must legally be (data residency), latency to users, service and VM size availability (new features appear in some regions first), price (it differs per region) and pairing/disaster recovery needs.

Example: a German health customer forces Germany West Central; a global SaaS picks the region nearest the biggest user group and adds a second one for recovery.

IaaS is right when you need control that PaaS does not give you: a legacy application that needs a specific OS, installed agents or drivers, or a licence tied to a machine.

Example: a 15-year-old Windows service that reads from a local COM component cannot run in App Service, so you rehost it on a VM now and plan to modernise later. You then patch the OS, secure it and back it up yourself.

Container Apps is usually called serverless containers: it is a managed platform (PaaS-like) where you ship a container and it can scale to zero and bill per use, without you running a Kubernetes cluster.

The labels overlap. What matters in an answer: you do not manage nodes, scaling rules (HTTP, queue length, KEDA) are built in, and you pay for use on the consumption profile, but you can also pick dedicated workload profiles for steady load.

code.title: Control plane vs data plane permission check

followUps:
Owner can do everything Contributor can and can assign roles to others (and manage policy assignments). Contributor can create, change and delete resources but cannot grant access.

That is why Owner on a subscription is dangerous: an Owner can give themselves or anyone else access. Prefer Contributor, or a narrower role at the resource-group scope. Neither role grants data-plane access to, say, Key Vault secrets or blobs (unless the account uses keys).

Use Privileged Identity Management (PIM): people are eligible for a role, request it with a reason, and it expires after a set time (for example 4 hours), with an optional approval and an audit trail.

The alternative of adding someone to a permanent Owner group is the habit to avoid. For production, keep daily accounts at Reader and let the engineer activate Contributor only during an incident.

Write a custom role only when no built-in role matches and a broader one gives too much power. The role is a list of allowed (and excluded) actions plus assignable scopes.

Example: a support team needs to restart Function Apps but not change settings. Built-in Contributor is too wide, so you create a role with Microsoft.Web/sites/restart/action and read actions. Keep custom roles few; each one is something you must maintain.

Example: security says encrypt everything with customer-managed keys, inspect traffic with a firewall and use private endpoints, but each hop and each key call adds latency.

A 10 ms Key Vault round-trip on every request can double the response time; the usual fix is caching the key or secret in memory and refreshing it on a timer. Trade-offs are decided with numbers: write down the target (p95 under 300 ms) and test the secure design against it.

The honest answer names a real weak spot and what you are doing about it. A common one is operational excellence (manual deployments, little documentation) or reliability (no tested recovery).

Example: "Reliability. We have backups but never restored one, so we do not know our real recovery time. I have scheduled a restore drill this quarter." A specific, fixable gap sounds stronger than saying everything is fine.

When the work is steady and high: Consumption pricing charges per execution and per second of memory, so at constant heavy load a fixed App Service or Premium plan is cheaper.

Rough example: if a function runs almost all day, you pay for nearly every second; a small dedicated instance at a flat monthly price wins. Also compare the cost of the supporting pieces (storage, networking), not only compute. Calculate with your real traffic, not averages.

Choose AKS when you need Kubernetes itself: custom operators, service mesh, fine control of networking and nodes, GPU scheduling, or a platform team that already runs Kubernetes.

Container Apps covers most microservice needs (revisions, scale rules, Dapr) with far less to operate. The cost of AKS is people: upgrades, node pools and security are yours. If nobody on the team wants to be a Kubernetes admin, stay on Container Apps.

Small team: pick the most managed service (Functions, App Service, Container Apps), because every extra thing to operate takes a share of a few people's time.

Large platform team: they can run AKS and offer a paved road. The right answer is not the most powerful tool, it is the tool the team can run well at 3 a.m. Say that, then give one example of each size.

Avoid an output binding when you need control: handling a partial failure, sending many messages in batches, setting message properties, returning the result of the send, or reusing a long-lived client with custom retry.

Example: you must send 500 messages and know which failed. With the Service Bus SDK you can send batches and catch errors; a binding just writes what you return. Bindings are great for simple one-in, one-out cases and less code.

Timer triggers use a six-field NCRONTAB expression: {second} {minute} {hour} {day} {month} {day-of-week}.

Examples: 0 */5 * * * * is every 5 minutes, and 0 30 9 * * 1-5 is 09:30 on weekdays. The time zone is UTC unless you set WEBSITE_TIME_ZONE. Mixing it up with the five-field Linux cron is the classic mistake.

No. A function has exactly one trigger, because the trigger defines why it runs. It can have many input and output bindings.

If two events should run the same logic, create two small functions that call a shared method. Example: OnQueueMessage and OnHttpRetry both call OrderService.Process(order).

local.settings.json holds your local app settings and connection strings (it is not deployed and should not be committed with secrets). host.json holds runtime behaviour that is deployed with the app: logging levels, retry, queue batch size, concurrency.

Example: AzureWebJobsStorage goes in local.settings.json locally (and in app settings in Azure); "maxConcurrentCalls": 8 for Service Bus goes in host.json.

Run the function host locally (func start or F5) against the Azurite storage emulator or a dev Service Bus, drop a message in the queue, and attach the debugger with a breakpoint in the handler.

For a message that already failed in Azure, copy its body into the local queue to reproduce it. Keep the handler logic in a normal class so you can also unit test it without the host.

You pay for instances that sit warm even when no requests arrive. That is the price of removing cold starts.

Example: on Flex Consumption, 2 always-ready instances bill their memory time all month, even at 3 a.m. on a Sunday. Set the lowest number that meets your latency goal, and only for the functions that are user-facing; keep batch and timer functions on scale-to-zero.

Flex Consumption, Premium and Dedicated (App Service) plans support virtual network integration. The old Linux/Windows Consumption plan does not support full VNet integration.

That is often the deciding point: if the function must reach a private-only database or Key Vault, you need Flex Consumption or Premium. Check this before you promise a design that needs private networking.

Move to Flex Consumption (Microsoft's recommended serverless plan) in steps: create a new Flex app, move app settings and identities, deploy the same code, test with traffic, then switch triggers and DNS.

Do not edit in place: triggers share a storage account, so run the old and new apps with different consumer names or disable the old triggers when you cut over, to avoid two apps processing the same message. Keep the old app for a rollback window.

code.title: Middleware pipeline that adds a correlation id

followUps:
Typical changes: the project becomes a console-style app with Program.cs and a host builder, usings change from Microsoft.Azure.WebJobs to Microsoft.Azure.Functions.Worker, attributes are renamed, ILogger comes from injection, and HTTP triggers use HttpRequestData or ASP.NET Core integration types.

Also check that every NuGet package you used works out of process, and re-test dependency versions: the worker has its own assembly context, so version conflicts with the host go away, which is the point of the move.

Write a function middleware registered in Program.cs with UseMiddleware<CorrelationMiddleware>(). It reads x-correlation-id from the request headers (or creates a GUID), puts it in the logging scope, and adds it to the response.

using (logger.BeginScope(new Dictionary<string,object> { ["CorrelationId"] = id }))
    await next(context);

This runs for every invocation, which is not possible with the old in-process model.

code.title: Static in-memory cache differs per instance

followUps:
Almost always because a new HttpClient is created for every call. Each one opens its own sockets, and closed sockets stay in TIME_WAIT for minutes, so you run out of ports (SNAT ports on Azure outbound).

Fix: create one long-lived client or use IHttpClientFactory injected through DI, and reuse SDK clients as singletons. Example: 200 calls per second with new clients each time can exhaust the roughly 128 preallocated SNAT ports per instance in seconds.

Set the maximum scale-out per app. On Flex Consumption use the maximum instance count setting; on Premium use the plan's maximum burst; on the old Consumption plan use WEBSITE_MAX_DYNAMIC_APPLICATION_SCALE_OUT. For queue triggers also lower the batch/concurrency in host.json.

Why: protect a downstream database that can only take, say, 50 concurrent connections: 10 instances x 5 concurrent calls = 50.

Because every instance has its own memory, and instances start, stop and scale at will. The cache may be empty after a restart and different on each instance, so users can see different data and invalidation is impossible.

Use a static cache only for safe, rarely changing, small data you can reload (for example a parsed config file). For shared data use Redis. The demo program shows two instances disagreeing after a change.

code.title: Idempotent handler with retries and dead-letter

followUps:
Make running the same message twice produce the same final state. Give every message a stable idempotency key (the message id or business key) and record it together with the side effect.

Example: INSERT INTO Payments(MessageId, ...) with a unique index on MessageId, in the same transaction as the update. A second delivery hits the unique constraint and you treat it as already done. Setting a value ("status = Paid") is naturally idempotent; "balance += 10" is not.

Fix the cause first (bad code, missing data). Then read the messages from the dead-letter sub-queue and resubmit them to the main queue, after checking they are safe to run again.

Tools: Service Bus Explorer in the portal, or a small admin function that receives from queue/$deadletterqueue and sends a copy to the queue. Resubmit in small batches, and rely on idempotency to avoid double effects.

When retrying cannot succeed: invalid input, a business rule failure, or a message that is simply malformed (a "poison" message). Retrying wastes capacity and delays the others.

Catch it, log the reason, and move it to the dead-letter queue yourself (or complete it and store an error record). Let the exception bubble up only for transient failures such as timeouts or a 503 from a dependency.

code.title: Check roles and scopes on a validated token

followUps:
Not on its own for a public API. A function key is a shared secret, not an identity: it cannot tell you who the user is, it is easily leaked, and rotating it breaks every caller.

Use it only for simple service-to-service cases. For a public API put Microsoft Entra ID (OAuth 2.0) in front, validate the token, and use AuthorizationLevel.Anonymous in the function while the platform or your code checks the token. Add API Management for throttling and keys per consumer.

Make the function reachable only from the gateway: use access restrictions to allow only APIM or Front Door (by IP/service tag, and check the X-Azure-FDID header for Front Door), or put the function behind a private endpoint with the gateway in the same network.

Also validate the token inside the function, so even if someone finds the default azurewebsites.net URL, they cannot get through without a valid token.

Validate the token first (signature, issuer, audience, expiry), then read the scp claim (delegated scopes, space separated) or the roles claim (app roles) from the ClaimsPrincipal and compare with what the operation needs.

if (!user.HasClaim("scp", "Orders.Read")
    && !user.IsInRole("Orders.Admin"))
    return Forbid();   // 403, not 401

The program above shows the order of checks: authentication gives 401, missing permission gives 403.

code.title: Orchestrator replay: deterministic, with stored results

followUps:
The new code can break the running instances: the orchestrator replays from history, and if the order of activities in the code no longer matches the history you get a non-determinism error.

Safe ways: use a new orchestration name or task hub version for the new code and let old instances finish, or make only compatible changes (inside activities, not the sequence). Treat orchestrator code like a stored contract.

Do not start all 10,000 activities at once. Process them in batches (for example 100 at a time, await the batch, then start the next), or use a sub-orchestration per chunk, and set maxConcurrentActivityFunctions in host.json.

foreach (var chunk in items.Chunk(100))
    await Task.WhenAll(chunk.Select(i =>
        ctx.CallActivityAsync("Process", i)));

This protects downstream systems and keeps the history table small.

Durable Functions when you want workflows in code with loops, branches and parallel steps, written and tested by developers. Logic Apps when the flow is mostly connecting SaaS services with ready connectors, or non-developers will maintain it. A Service Bus saga (messages plus state) when steps are in different services and teams and you want loose coupling.

Example: approval flow with timers and human events inside one app: Durable. Salesforce to SharePoint sync: Logic Apps.

Because if someone breaks into the application, running as root gives them far more power inside the container (and sometimes a way out to the host). A non-root user limits the damage.

In a Dockerfile add USER app (the .NET images already ship a non-root app user and listen on port 8080). Many platforms and policies also reject containers that run as root.

Liveness asks "is this process stuck?": if it fails, the platform restarts the container. Readiness asks "can this instance take traffic now?": if it fails, the instance is taken out of the load balancer but not restarted.

Example: while the app warms up its cache, readiness fails so users are not sent there. Keep liveness cheap and do not call the database in it, or a database outage will restart all your containers.

Container Apps scales with KEDA rules: HTTP concurrent requests, queue length, CPU/memory, or custom event sources. You set min and max replicas and a rule such as "1 replica per 50 concurrent requests".

Example: a queue worker with rule "1 replica per 10 messages" and max 20: with 95 messages it runs 10 replicas, and with an empty queue it scales to zero if min is 0.

Do not bake environment values into the bundle. Build once, then load settings at runtime from a small config.json (or an API call) that is fetched when the app starts, and replace that file per environment at deploy time.

Example: fetch('/config.json') returns {"apiUrl":"https://api.example/test"}. The same built files then go to test and production, so what you tested is what you ship.

In staticwebapp.config.json under globalHeaders, or at the edge with Front Door rules. Example: "Content-Security-Policy": "default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'".

Start in report-only mode to see what would break, then enforce. Avoid 'unsafe-inline'; use nonces or hashes for inline scripts.

Pick Blob static website plus Front Door when you need more control or scale of the edge: custom WAF rules, several origins (one domain for the site and APIs), advanced caching and routing, or very large traffic. It also fits when the site is just files with no auth or API proxy features.

Static Web Apps is simpler (built-in auth, routing, API proxy, preview environments per pull request); Blob plus Front Door gives you more knobs and more things to configure.

The platform warms the new slot (the staging instances start and are checked), then switches the routing so production traffic goes to the new code, and the old code moves into the staging slot. No restart for users because the instances are already warm.

Slot-specific settings stay with the slot, other settings move with the code. If the new version is bad, swap again to go back in seconds.

Settings that are different per environment and must not travel with the code: the connection string of the environment, a slot-specific feature flag, or the setting that disables background jobs in staging.

Example: ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT and the staging database connection string are slot settings; the app version number and normal feature defaults are not. If you forget, the swap sends the staging database string to production.

Scale up means a bigger machine (more CPU and memory, by changing the plan tier, e.g. from P1v3 to P2v3). Scale out means more instances of the same size, shared behind a load balancer, manually or by autoscale rules.

Scale out is the usual answer for traffic; it needs the app to be stateless. Scale up helps for a single heavy request or memory-hungry work. Example: CPU 80% on 2 instances, so add instances; one big report runs out of memory, so scale up.

Table Storage is enough when you only need cheap key-value lookups by a partition and row key, with simple data and no complex queries or global distribution. It costs a fraction of Cosmos DB.

Example: storing audit records or device status by DeviceId and timestamp. Use Cosmos DB when you need richer queries, secondary indexes, guaranteed low latency worldwide or multi-region writes.

Files are large, change the database size, bloat backups and make queries and restores slower; you also pay premium database prices for storage that blob storage offers for a few cents per GB.

Store the file in Blob Storage and keep only the URL or blob name in the database. Give users a short-lived SAS link to download directly from storage. Small data (under a few KB, like a signature) can stay in the row.

Cosmos DB when you need global distribution, single-digit-millisecond reads at large scale, flexible JSON documents and automatic horizontal partitioning; Azure SQL when you have relational data, joins, transactions across tables and reporting.

Example: a product catalogue read worldwide, one document per product: Cosmos. Orders with invoices and payments that must be consistent: Azure SQL. Do not pick Cosmos just because it sounds modern.

Only with RA-GRS or RA-GZRS (read-access). Plain GRS keeps a copy in the paired region but you cannot read it until Microsoft or you fail over.

With read access you get a second endpoint (account-secondary.blob...) for reads, but data there may be slightly behind, because replication is asynchronous (RPO is typically under 15 minutes, not zero).

Archive blobs are offline: you cannot read them directly. You must first rehydrate them to Hot or Cool, which can take hours (standard priority up to 15 hours, high priority under 1 hour for small blobs).

There is also an early-deletion charge if you remove or move a blob before 180 days. Use archive for data you almost never need, such as old compliance records.

Yes, and it is common. Event Grid reacts to an event (for example, a blob was created) and routes it to a Service Bus queue, where the consumer processes it reliably with retries, dead-lettering and sessions.

Event Grid is good at pushing small notifications; Service Bus is good at holding work until someone handles it. Together: "file uploaded" event, then a durable queue of jobs.

An Event Hub is split into partitions. A consumer group is an independent view of the whole stream with its own read position. Two apps (analytics and alerting) use two consumer groups and each reads every event.

Inside one consumer group, partitions are shared among the instances, so max parallelism equals the number of partitions. Each consumer tracks its offset (checkpoint) separately.

Kafka when you already run Kafka, need its ecosystem (Connect, Streams, schema tooling), exactly the Kafka protocol, or portability across clouds.

Event Hubs also exposes a Kafka-compatible endpoint, so many Kafka clients work without changes. If you only need high-volume ingestion on Azure, Event Hubs saves you from running a cluster.

code.title: Service Bus lock expiry, delivery count and dead-letter

followUps:
No. Duplicate detection only drops a message with the same MessageId sent again within a time window (up to 7 days), which protects against sender retries.

The consumer can still receive a message twice (lock expiry, crash after the work but before completing). So handlers must be idempotent. Real exactly-once effect = duplicate detection on send + idempotent processing on receive.

The lock expires, the message becomes available again, and another consumer (or the same one) processes it a second time. When you then try to complete the first attempt you get a MessageLockLost error. After the max delivery count it goes to the dead-letter queue.

Fixes: lock renewal (the SDK processor does it automatically up to MaxAutoLockRenewalDuration), a longer lock duration, or splitting the work. The program above shows the effect.

The outbox pattern: in the same database transaction as your business change, write the message into an Outbox table. A separate publisher reads that table and sends to Service Bus, then marks the row sent.

Without it, you can save the order but crash before sending the message (or send and fail to save). The outbox makes saving and sending atomic from the outside, with at-least-once delivery, which pairs with idempotent consumers.

code.title: Cache-aside with expiry and a stampede guard

followUps:
HybridCache (in .NET 9 and later) combines a fast in-process L1 cache with the distributed L2 cache (Redis) behind one API, and adds stampede protection (only one caller loads a missing key), serialization, and tag-based invalidation.

With IDistributedCache you write the get, miss, load, set and locking code yourself. With HybridCache: await cache.GetOrCreateAsync(key, ct => LoadAsync(ct)).

Use tags (HybridCache supports removing by tag) or versioned keys: include a version number in the key (product:v7:42) and bump the version to make every old key unreachable; they expire on their own.

Avoid scanning with KEYS * in production, since it blocks Redis. Example: all keys for tenant 5 share the tag tenant:5; one call removes them.

Never cache secrets or passwords in a shared cache, personal data without need and encryption, per-user results under a shared key (a data leak between users), or anything where stale data causes harm, like an account balance used for payment.

Also do not cache errors for long. Example bug: caching "user profile" under the key profile instead of profile:{userId} shows one user's data to everyone.

code.title: Partition key choice and hot partitions

followUps:
A request unit (RU) is Cosmos DB's currency for the cost of an operation (CPU, memory, I/O). A point read of a 1 KB item by id and partition key costs 1 RU; queries cost more.

Lower the cost by: always including the partition key in the query (avoid cross-partition fan-out), reading by id when you can, indexing only needed paths, selecting only the fields you need, and keeping items small.

You cannot change the partition key of an existing container in place. Options: create a new container with a better key (for example a synthetic key like tenantId_hash(0..9)) and migrate with the change feed or the container copy tool, then switch the app.

Short-term relief: raise throughput, or move the largest tenant to its own container. Check the hot key with the metrics for normalized RU consumption per partition.

The change feed is an ordered log of inserts and updates per partition (not deletes by default) that you can read and process later.

Uses: update a search index or a materialized view, publish events to Service Bus, trigger an Azure Function, migrate data to another container. It is the safe way to react to data changes without polling.

Choose a user-assigned managed identity when several resources should share one identity and one set of permissions, when you want to create and authorise the identity before the resource exists (in IaC), or when the identity should survive redeploys of the resource.

System-assigned is simpler and dies with the resource. Example: five Function Apps that all read the same Key Vault share one user-assigned identity with a single role assignment.

The app setting holds a reference like @Microsoft.KeyVault(SecretUri=https://my-vault.vault.azure.net/secrets/DbPassword/). App Service or Functions resolves it at startup using the app's managed identity, so your code reads a normal setting and never sees the Key Vault API.

The identity needs Key Vault Secrets User. Without a version in the URI the value refreshes automatically (within about a day), and a failure to resolve shows up in the portal as a reference error.

Use the App Configuration provider with a sentinel key and refresh: you register a Refresh on a key like Sentinel, add the middleware, and the app re-reads all settings when the sentinel changes (checked on a cache interval, default 30 seconds).

The Microsoft.FeatureManagement library then reads flags through IFeatureManager, so flipping a flag in the portal takes effect without a restart.

code.title: Credential chain: try each source in order

followUps:
Locally you used your own account, which has access; in Azure the managed identity is a different principal with no role yet. A 403 almost always means a missing role assignment.

Check: is the managed identity enabled; does it have the right data-plane role (for example Key Vault Secrets User, Storage Blob Data Reader) at the right scope; did the assignment finish (it can take minutes); is a firewall or private endpoint blocking the call; for user-assigned identities, was the client id supplied?

Because it tries many sources in order and can pick an unexpected one, which is slow, hard to debug and sometimes insecure (an environment variable on a build server wins over the managed identity). The failure messages list every attempted source, which is noisy.

In production prefer a specific credential such as ManagedIdentityCredential (or exclude sources with options). Keep DefaultAzureCredential for local development convenience.

code.title: Rate limit per customer key with a token bucket

followUps:
Use the rate-limit-by-key policy with a key expression that identifies the customer, such as the subscription id or a claim from the token, instead of context.Request.IpAddress.

<rate-limit-by-key calls="100" renewal-period="60"
  counter-key="@(context.Subscription.Id)" />

IP is a poor key because many customers share one office or NAT address, and one customer may use many IPs. Different products or tiers can have different limits.

Lock the back end so that only APIM can reach it: private endpoint or VNet integration plus IP restrictions, or APIM adds a secret header or sends a managed identity token that the back end validates.

Without that, anyone who discovers the back end's own URL can skip all APIM policies (auth, throttling, logging). Check the back end's token audience too.

A version is a public, breaking-change line of your API (v1, v2) that clients choose, via path, header or query. A revision is a non-breaking change made safely behind the same version: you edit a revision, test it, then make it current, and can roll back.

Example: adding an optional field is a new revision of v1; removing a field means a new version v2.

Front Door is global: it sits at the Microsoft edge, gives anycast routing, CDN caching, WAF and failover between regions. Application Gateway is regional: a layer 7 load balancer inside one virtual network, good for private back ends and path routing in one region.

Common design: Front Door in front for global entry and WAF, Application Gateway or private origins behind it for regional routing.

Through VNet integration for outbound traffic from the function and a private endpoint on the database, with a private DNS zone so the database name resolves to its private IP.

Steps: put the app in a VNet-integrated plan (Flex Consumption or Premium), create the private endpoint in the same or peered VNet, link the privatelink DNS zone, then disable public access on the database.

Build agents on the public internet can no longer reach private-only resources, so deployments, tests and migrations fail.

Solutions: use self-hosted agents or Azure DevOps scale-set agents in the VNet, or managed DevOps pools with VNet injection. Plan this early, since it changes the cost and the set-up of every pipeline stage that touches private resources.

Adding a private endpoint does not by itself turn off the public path; this message shows public access was disabled and your client is still using the public IP. Usually the DNS is not resolving to the private IP.

Check the private DNS zone (for example privatelink.database.windows.net) is linked to the client's VNet, and run nslookup from the app: it must return a 10.x address. Also confirm the app has VNet integration with route-all or the right DNS settings.

Put agents inside (or peered with) the VNet: self-hosted agents on a VM scale set, containers in the VNet, or Microsoft-managed pools with VNet injection. They resolve the private DNS name and use the private endpoint.

For one-off administration, use a jump host or Azure Bastion. Avoid re-enabling public access "just for the pipeline"; that opens the door you closed.

A metric is a number measured over time (CPU %, requests per second): cheap, fast, ideal for alerts and dashboards. A log is a record of one event with details (an exception with a stack trace): rich, bigger, and searched with queries.

Use metrics to notice a problem ("error rate is 5%"), then logs to find the cause ("which exception and which request").

Sampling keeps only a fraction of telemetry (for example 20% of requests) to cut cost and volume. Metrics computed before sampling stay correct; counting the stored items yourself does not.

It misleads when you look for a rare failure: 1 error in 1,000 can vanish. Keep exceptions at 100%, use adaptive sampling carefully, and remember a sampled-out request has no trace to look at.

Business events that tell you if the product works, not just if servers run: order placed, payment failed, login blocked, import finished with a duration and count.

Give each event a few useful dimensions (tenant, result, plan), never personal data or secrets, and a stable name. Example: PaymentFailed with reason=card_declined lets you chart failures by reason.

code.title: SLO, error budget and burn rate

followUps:
Because a liveness check decides "restart me". If the database has an outage, every instance fails liveness at once and gets restarted in a loop, which makes the outage worse and adds a restart storm when the database returns.

Liveness should only check the process itself (can it answer a trivial request). Put dependency checks in readiness, where failing just removes the instance from traffic.

Alert on symptoms users feel (error rate, latency against the SLO), not on every cause like CPU 70%. Each alert must need a human action; if an alert is routinely ignored, delete or fix it.

Use burn-rate alerts, group related ones, set severity levels (page vs ticket), add a runbook link, and review noisy alerts every month. A page at 3 a.m. should always matter.

Start from the user journey: pick one or two SLIs (availability of the main API, and p95 latency), measure the current numbers for a few weeks, then set an SLO slightly below what you already deliver, for example 99.5%.

Do not pick 99.99% because it sounds good: it allows only about 4 minutes of failure a month and will freeze every release. Tighten it later when the team has proven it can hold it.

code.title: Carry a trace id across a queue message

followUps:
Put the trace context in the message properties when you send (for Service Bus the SDK writes Diagnostic-Id / traceparent for you), and on receive start a new span with that parent.

Without it, the producer and consumer appear as two unrelated traces. Also copy your own business correlation id into the properties so you can search logs even without tracing tools.

Generate or accept a correlation id at the edge, store it in the logging scope, and return it in the error body and a response header, for example {"title":"Server error","traceId":"4bf92f35..."} (ProblemDetails already has a traceId extension).

Then a user can quote the id to support, and you search the logs for it. Never include the stack trace or internal details in what you show.

Sampling decides whether a whole trace is recorded. Good setups sample at the trace level (all spans of a request kept or dropped together) so you never see half a trace.

The catch: if 10% of traces are kept, the one request a user complains about is likely missing. Keep errors and slow requests (tail-based sampling), and allow forcing full capture for a given request.

code.title: Composite availability of serial and parallel parts

followUps:
Choose active-passive when the business accepts a few minutes of failover and wants lower cost and simpler data (one writer). Choose active-active when downtime must be near zero or users are global, accepting higher cost and hard problems like conflicting writes.

Decide from the numbers: recovery time objective (RTO), recovery point objective (RPO), budget and team skill. Most business apps do well with active-passive and a practised failover.

At least once or twice a year for a critical system, and after major architecture changes, with a written plan and a time measurement. Some teams do a small drill every quarter.

A failover plan that has never been run is a guess. The drill finds the missing DNS entry, the secret that does not exist in the second region, or the 6-hour restore you thought took 30 minutes.

Replication copies mistakes as well as good data: if someone deletes a table or a bug corrupts rows, the damage replicates to the second region within seconds. It also does not protect against ransomware or a bad deployment.

That is why you also need backups with point-in-time restore, soft delete, immutable storage and tested restores. Replication is for hardware and region failures; backups are for human and software failures.

Quota protects shared GPU capacity. It is limited as tokens per minute (and requests per minute) per deployment and region, so one customer cannot take all the capacity.

If your app goes over, you get HTTP 429. Plan with the expected tokens: 100 users x 2,000 tokens per request x 6 requests per minute = 1.2 million TPM. Ask for more quota, spread over regions, or use provisioned throughput for guarantees.

Start from the task: a small, cheap model for classification, extraction and simple chat; a larger one for complex reasoning, long documents or code. Then compare quality on your own test set, latency, cost per million tokens, context window, and region availability.

Run 50 to 100 real examples through two candidates, score them, and take the cheapest model that passes. Re-test when new versions appear.

Your prompts, completions and fine-tuning data stay within the Azure service in the region you chose; Microsoft does not use them to train the base models. But the prompt content is sent to the model (the deployment), so anything you put in it, including customer data, is processed there.

So send only what is needed, mask sensitive data, and check data zone / residency options, content logging settings and your contract.

code.title: Build and parse a chat request; validate JSON output

followUps:
For calls with Entra ID, the identity needs Cognitive Services OpenAI User (to run completions) on the Azure OpenAI resource. Use Cognitive Services OpenAI Contributor only for people or pipelines that manage deployments.

Assign it to the app's managed identity at the resource scope. A 401 or 403 after setup usually means the role is missing or has not propagated yet.

Streaming sends tokens as they are produced, so the user starts reading after a fraction of a second instead of waiting 10 to 20 seconds for the whole answer. It improves perceived speed; total time is about the same.

The cost: more complex code (server-sent events), harder content filtering and no chance to check the complete answer before the user sees part of it.

Use structured outputs with a JSON schema (the model is forced to match it), or at least JSON mode, set temperature low, and validate in code every time, since the model can still return the wrong values.

If validation fails, retry once with the error message in the prompt, then fall back to a safe default or a human. Never pass raw model output to a database or a shell. The program above rejects three bad replies.

Provisioned throughput (PTU) reserves model capacity for you at a fixed monthly price, giving predictable latency and no 429 from other tenants, instead of paying per token on shared capacity.

It pays off when traffic is steady and high: if the pay-as-you-go bill is larger than the reservation and you cannot tolerate latency spikes. For spiky or small usage it is wasteful.

Treat prompts like code: keep an evaluation set of 50 to 200 real examples with expected results, run old and new prompt on it, and compare scores (automatic checks plus an LLM or human grader). Then release gradually with a feature flag to a small share of users.

Watch the results, not a feeling: accuracy, refusal rate, cost, latency. Store prompts in version control.

Show a clear, polite, non-technical message such as "I cannot help with that request. Try rephrasing", and let them continue; do not show the raw filter category or an error code.

Log the event (without the personal text where possible) so you can see false positives. Give a way to report a wrong block, and keep the UI state so the user does not lose their input.

You need confidence without a human: a fast, reliable automated test suite, feature flags to separate deploy from release, good monitoring with automatic rollback, small changes, and a deployment that is repeatable and tested.

Also a safe database migration approach and a team culture that fixes a failing pipeline first. If you cannot roll back in minutes, keep the approval.

Aim for under 10 minutes for the pull request build and tests (many teams say 5 to 10). Longer than that and people stop waiting, batch their changes, and merge bigger, riskier pull requests.

Keep it fast by running tests in parallel, caching dependencies, running only affected tests, and moving slow end-to-end tests to a nightly or post-merge stage.

Create a hotfix branch from the release tag or the production commit (not from main), fix and test there, deploy it, and then merge or cherry-pick the fix back into main so it is not lost.

With trunk-based development and feature flags, you avoid the problem: main is always releasable, and unfinished work is hidden behind a flag.

The longer a branch lives, the more it drifts, so merges become painful, conflicts large, reviews huge, and integration bugs appear late. Others build on code that is changing under them.

Fix it by merging small changes daily (trunk-based), using feature flags for unfinished work, and rebasing or merging main into the branch often. A branch older than a week is a warning sign.

Use naming and automation: branch names like feature/1234-add-invoice-export and commit or pull request text with AB#1234 (Azure Boards) or #1234 (GitHub). The tool then links the work item, the pull request and the deployment.

Add a branch policy that requires a linked work item, so every change can be traced back to a reason.

A reasonable gate is around 70 to 80% on new code, not a high number for the whole project. Coverage tells you what is not tested, but not whether the tests are good: 100% can still miss every bug.

Requiring coverage on new code stops the number falling without forcing painful tests for old code. Pair it with review of test quality, and add mutation testing for critical logic.

Have an explicit break-glass path: a named approver (tech lead or on-call) can override the gate, the reason is recorded, and a follow-up ticket fixes the cause. The urgent fix still goes through the build and the tests that matter.

Do not disable the gate for everyone or let it become normal. If a gate blocks often for false reasons, the gate is wrong and needs fixing.

Measure first: track which tests fail and pass on re-run. Quarantine a flaky test (still runs, but does not block), assign an owner and a deadline to fix or delete it.

Common causes: shared state, time dependence, real network calls, random ordering, async waits with fixed sleeps. Do not just add automatic retries for everything; that hides real bugs and slows the build.

code.title: Detect drift between desired and actual resources

followUps:
Drift is when the real environment no longer matches the code, usually because someone changed it by hand in the portal during an incident.

Detect it with a plan/preview run on a schedule (terraform plan or az deployment group what-if with an alert on any change), and with Azure Policy. Fix by changing the code to accept the change, or re-applying the code. Reduce it by giving people read-only access in production.

In a remote backend, typically an Azure Storage blob container with locking, versioning and access limited to the pipeline identity. Never keep state in git or on a laptop.

State may contain secrets (passwords, keys) in plain text and is the source of truth for what exists; if it is lost or corrupted, Terraform may recreate or duplicate resources. Enable soft delete and blob versions.

Write modules that take inputs (name, size, sku) and produce the resources, and keep one set of parameter files per environment: dev.tfvars, test.tfvars, prod.tfvars (or Bicep .bicepparam files).

The same module code deploys to all three, only parameters differ (a small SKU in dev, zone redundancy in prod). Version modules and test them, so a change moves through dev first.

Approvals and checks on an environment are managed outside the YAML by the people who own that environment, so a developer cannot remove the approval by editing the pipeline file in their own branch.

The same pipeline can then deploy to test without a wait and to production only after an approver (and optionally a business-hours check) signs off. That is separation of duties.

When the agent must reach resources that are not on the public internet (private endpoints, on-premises systems), when you need special software or a large machine, long builds that benefit from persistent caches, or fixed IPs for firewall rules.

The price: you patch, secure and scale them yourself. Microsoft-hosted agents are simpler when none of that applies.

Put shared steps in a template repository and reference it: resources: repositories: plus template: build-dotnet.yml@templates. Use parameters for the differences and pin a tag or branch version.

Changes to the template then reach 10 pipelines at once, so version it, test it, and require review, since a mistake there breaks everyone.

A wrong tag can ship the wrong product, version or commit, and anyone with write access can push a tag and trigger a release.

Guards: protected tags (only release managers can create v*), the workflow checks that the tag points to a commit on main, it checks the version format, the production job needs an environment approval, and tag naming includes the product (orders-v1.4.0).

Build the artifact once (on the tag or on main), upload it as a workflow artifact or to a registry with the commit SHA, and let each environment deploy that same artifact. Never rebuild for production.

Configuration comes from the environment at deploy time. Then the thing tested in staging is byte-for-byte what reaches production.

Use path filters (on.push.paths) or a changed-files step (such as dorny/paths-filter) to detect which folders changed, and run only those jobs. Build tools with an affected-projects graph help for large monorepos.

Example: a change only under apps/billing/** triggers the billing tests, not the orders ones. Run everything on main before release so the filters cannot hide a shared-library break.

code.title: Federated credential: match issuer, subject and audience

followUps:
The subject says exactly which repository, and which branch, tag, environment or pull request the job runs for, for example repo:contoso/shop:environment:production. Entra ID only gives a token if the subject matches the federated credential you configured.

It matters because a broad subject (any branch) lets any workflow in the repo act as that identity. Use the narrowest subject: the production environment, protected by approvals.

They can change what the job does with the identity: if the job's subject matches (for example the same branch or environment), the edited workflow can run any command with that identity's permissions, such as reading secrets or deleting resources.

Defence: bind the production identity to an environment with required reviewers, protect branches, require review for changes to workflow files (CODEOWNERS), and give the identity minimum roles.

Use two identities (two app registrations or managed identities), each with a federated credential for its own environment subject and roles on its own subscription only.

The test identity has no rights at all in production. Then even a compromised test workflow cannot touch production, and production needs the protected environment with approvals.

code.title: Canary: stable percentage rollout by user id

followUps:
You cannot undo the data change by redeploying code, so you restore from a backup or point-in-time restore, or write a compensating script, and accept lost data created after the migration.

Better: avoid destructive steps in one release. Use expand and contract: add the new column, deploy code that writes both, backfill, switch reads, and drop the old column only a release or two later, once you know you will not roll back.

Slot swap (blue-green) switches 100% of traffic at once and rolls back instantly: simple, good when you can test the staging slot well. Canary sends a small share (1% to 10%) of real users first and increases step by step: better when real traffic is the only true test or the blast radius must be small.

Canary needs routing control and good monitoring; slot swap needs only App Service slots.

Treat each flag as a temporary item: give it an owner, a purpose and an expiry date when it is created, list flags in a dashboard, and add a ticket to remove it when the rollout reaches 100%.

Review stale flags monthly and fail the build (or warn) on flags past their date. Permanent settings like entitlements should be configuration, not flags.

Use just-in-time access: the engineer requests production access through PIM with a ticket reference, it needs approval, lasts a few hours and is logged, then it expires on its own.

Prefer read-only access and diagnostics tools first (logs, Application Insights). Changes go through the pipeline whenever possible; direct changes are exceptions that you review afterwards.

Use synthetic or anonymised data: generate fake records with the same shape and volume, or copy production and mask names, emails, and ids with a repeatable script, run in a protected place before it reaches test.

Never copy raw personal data to test (privacy law, weaker security). Keep a small reusable seed set for automated tests and a larger generated set for performance tests.

As few as meet your needs: typically dev (or local), test/staging, production; add a separate performance or pre-production environment only if you use it. Each environment costs money, needs maintenance and slows everything when they drift.

Too many shows in symptoms: nobody knows which one is current, "works in UAT, fails in staging" stories, and queues for a shared environment. Prefer short-lived preview environments created per pull request.

code.title: Monthly cost estimate: serverless vs fixed plan

followUps:
Pick a real, specific example: a Log Analytics workspace ingesting verbose debug logs (hundreds of GB a month), an idle Premium plan or Cosmos DB with high provisioned RU, NAT or egress traffic, or a forgotten test environment.

You find these in Cost Analysis by grouping by resource and meter, then drilling into the daily graph for a jump. Fix: lower log levels or sampling, scale down or shut off, add budgets and alerts.

When the load is high and steady. Pay-per-use is cheap for spiky or small workloads, but a service busy 24/7 pays for every second, so a fixed plan with reserved capacity wins. Cold-start workarounds (always-ready instances) also reduce the savings.

The program shows a break-even: above roughly a given number of executions a month the fixed plan is cheaper. Calculate with your real traffic.

Write down the load assumptions (users, requests per second, data size, growth), list each component with its pricing meter, and use the Azure Pricing Calculator. Then add a margin for logs, egress, backup and non-production environments.

Give a range (best, expected, worst), mark the assumptions, and validate with a small proof of concept and a budget alert after launch.

code.title: Average vs p95 latency: why averages hide slow requests

followUps:
Common reasons: test has little data, production has millions of rows so a missing index or a full scan hurts; a different execution plan from outdated statistics or parameter sniffing; locks or blocking from real concurrency; a smaller pricing tier in production.

Check the actual execution plan and Query Store for the regression, compare plans, and test with production-sized data. Fix with an index, updated statistics or a query rewrite.

Roll back when the impact is large, the cause is unknown, and rollback is safe and fast (a slot swap takes seconds). Fix forward when the cause is clear and tiny, the fix is quick to test, or rollback is risky (the database already changed).

Rule of thumb: stop the bleeding first. Roll back, then investigate calmly, unless rollback itself is not possible.

Add a performance gate: a short load test against the staging slot that compares p95 latency and error rate with a baseline and fails the stage if it is more than, say, 20% worse. Also run smoke tests after deployment and a canary stage with automatic rollback on an alert.

Keep a dashboard annotation for each deployment so the cause is visible immediately.

Use continuous replication: Azure Database Migration Service (or log shipping / transactional replication) copies the database while the old system still runs. At cut-over you stop writes briefly, let the last changes catch up, switch the connection string, and verify.

Downtime then is minutes, not hours. Practise the whole cut-over in a rehearsal and write a rollback plan: the old database stays intact until you are sure.

The strangler fig pattern replaces an old system piece by piece: put a routing layer (gateway or proxy) in front, build one feature in the new system, route that URL to it, and repeat until the old system has nothing left and can be switched off.

It avoids a risky big-bang rewrite: each step is small, delivers value and can be rolled back. Example: move /invoices first, leave /reports on the old app.

Rehost (lift and shift) when you have a hard deadline (data centre closing, support ending), the app is stable and rarely changes, or the code cannot be changed (no source, no skills). It is the fastest and lowest risk way to get out.

The cost: you keep the old design and may pay more than PaaS. Plan to modernise afterwards; do not leave it as the final state forever.

code.title: Tenant isolation: always filter by tenant id

followUps:
Three levels, from cheapest to strongest: a shared database with a tenant id column on every table (use a global query filter and row-level security), a schema per tenant, or a database per tenant (best isolation, per-tenant restore, more cost and operations).

Choose by customer needs: many small tenants get shared tables, large or regulated ones get their own database. The tenant id comes from the token, never from client input.

Usually the database (connections, writes, a single hot table or partition) or a shared dependency like a rate-limited external API, before the stateless API instances, which scale out easily.

Find it by load testing: watch DTU/CPU, locks, connection pool use and queue lengths. Typical fixes: caching, read replicas, indexes, queues to smooth writes, partitioning.

Deploy a separate stamp (a full copy of the application and data) in the region the customer requires, with its own database, storage, keys and logs, and make sure backups, telemetry and AI calls also stay in that region.

Route that tenant to its stamp with a global directory. Check hidden data flows: monitoring workspaces, support tools, and any region-pairing for disaster recovery that would copy data abroad.

Settings that differ per environment and must stay with the slot when you swap: connection strings, environment name, slot-specific feature flags, and the setting that disables timers or queue triggers in staging.

For Functions, also mark AzureWebJobs.<FunctionName>.Disabled as a slot setting if staging should not process queues. Settings that describe the code (version, normal defaults) should move with the code.

Yes. Use identity-based connections: set AzureWebJobsStorage__accountName (or the blob/queue/table service URIs) and give the managed identity roles such as Storage Blob Data Owner, Storage Queue Data Contributor and Storage Table Data Contributor on the account.

This removes the storage key from app settings. Flex Consumption uses this model by default; check the role list for the triggers you use (Durable and queue triggers need more than blob roles).

A user delegation SAS is signed with Entra ID credentials (a delegation key obtained with a role) instead of the storage account key. It lasts a limited time (up to 7 days).

It is safer because the account key (full access, hard to rotate) is never used, the permissions can be traced to an identity, and revoking the delegation key or the role stops the SAS. Prefer it to account-key SAS.

Give the app's managed identity the AcrPull role on the container registry, and set the app to use the managed identity for registry authentication. No admin user or password is stored.

For Container Apps or App Service you pick "managed identity" in the registry settings; for AKS, attach the registry to the cluster so the kubelet identity gets AcrPull.

Blue-green is the easiest to roll back: the old environment is still running, so you flip the router back and users return at once. Canary is also easy: set the share to 0%. Both are far easier than rolling back an in-place update.

The hard part is the database: if the new version changed the schema in an incompatible way, neither strategy helps. Blue-green needs double capacity for a while; canary needs routing and monitoring.

Because the deployment name is only a label your code calls; the model behind it can differ per environment. You may use a cheaper or smaller model in dev and test, a newer model version in test to evaluate it, and the approved one in production.

That keeps code identical across environments, but test results may not predict production, so evaluate the exact production model before release.
